# Script Logging Demo

This runbook shows how a script logs at a level: by appending lines to the log files Runbooks creates for each run.

## The log files

Each run gets one log file per level, named by an environment variable:

| Variable | When to use it |
|----------|----------------|
| `RUNBOOK_INFO_LOG` | General progress messages, status updates |
| `RUNBOOK_WARN_LOG` | Non-fatal issues, deprecation notices |
| `RUNBOOK_ERROR_LOG` | Failures that will cause the script to exit |
| `RUNBOOK_DEBUG_LOG` | Verbose output for troubleshooting |

Runbooks shows each line appended to one of these files in the block's logs as `[timestamp] [LEVEL] message`, at the file's level. Plain `echo` output shows up too, without a level.

## See It In Action

Run this command to see a line at each level:

<Command 
    id="logging-demo" 
    path="scripts/logging-demo.sh"
    title="Run Logging Demo"
    description="Appends lines to each of the four log files"
    successMessage="Demo complete! Notice how each log level has a distinct prefix."
    failMessage="Demo failed unexpectedly"

## Debug Output

Runbooks shows every line in `$RUNBOOK_DEBUG_LOG`. To keep debug lines out of the logs unless someone asks for them, have the script decide whether to write them. This check writes debug lines only when its `DEBUG` variable is `true`.

Run this check with and without debug output to see the difference:

<Check 
    id="debug-check" 
    path="checks/debug-check.sh"
    env={{ DEBUG: "{{ .inputs.EnableDebug }}" }}
    title="Check with Debug Output"
    description="Run with DEBUG=true to see verbose output"
    successMessage="Check passed!"
    failMessage="Check failed"
>
    <Inputs id="debug-toggle">
    ```yaml
    variables:
      - name: EnableDebug
        type: bool
        description: "Write debug lines by setting `DEBUG=true` for this script run."
        default: false
    ```
    </Inputs>
</Check>

## Logging in Your Scripts

Append a line to the file for its level:

```bash
echo "Starting process..." >> "$RUNBOOK_INFO_LOG"
echo "Detailed variable state: $MY_VAR" >> "$RUNBOOK_DEBUG_LOG"
echo "Optional dependency not found, continuing anyway" >> "$RUNBOOK_WARN_LOG"
echo "Critical failure, exiting" >> "$RUNBOOK_ERROR_LOG"
```

Nothing written to the log files reaches stdout, so you can log inside a function whose output you capture with `$(...)`. A tool's stderr can go straight to a file, and its lines show up at that level:

```bash
tofu plan -no-color 2>>"$RUNBOOK_ERROR_LOG"
```

If you log often, define short functions in your own script, such as `info() { echo "$*" >> "$RUNBOOK_INFO_LOG"; }`. See [Logging](https://runbooks.gruntwork.io/authoring/blocks/command/#logging).
